claims.text: The damaged metallic component is vulnerable to hot cracking when repaired by fusion methods.
Cold spray using a pre-alloyed powder matching the substrate composition can repair the damaged component.
The powder should be deposited at particle velocities above 600 m/s.
Cold spray deposition is performed in an inert atmosphere at near-ambient temperature.
Peening or low-temperature annealing after deposition will densify the deposited layer and enhance bonding.
An inert processing atmosphere will avoid oxidation.
Dynamic plastic deformation during particle impact produces a densely consolidated, strain-hardened layer.
Post-deposition treatment further reduces residual porosity in the repair layer.
The kinetic energy of high-velocity particles causes severe plastic deformation upon impact.
Impact deformation promotes mechanical interlocking and solid-state bonding without melting.
Post-deposition treatment enhances the interfacial microstructure and continuity between the deposit and substrate.
Avoiding melting prevents fusion-induced hot cracking in the repair.
The repaired layer will have tensile strength comparable to or greater than that of the base material.
The repaired layer will have fatigue resistance comparable to or greater than that of the base material.
The two-step cold spray repair will outperform conventional fusion-weld repair.
The improved repair performance will persist under aggressive operating conditions.
Traditional fusion-welding repairs are prone to hot cracking and solidification-related microstructural defects.
Hot cracking and associated microstructural defects give fusion-weld repairs inferior long-term performance under aggressive conditions.
The process must remain below temperature thresholds that would induce deleterious phase transformations.
High-entropy alloys are examples of materials with a narrow fusion-processing window.

contradictions.description: Low-temperature annealing is presented as an example of a mechanical post-treatment, but annealing is a thermal treatment; the stated mechanism of further mechanical compaction therefore does not cover one of the proposed treatment alternatives.
